note: When Shammai the Elder's daughter-in-law gave birth to a son, Shammai broke away the plaster of the ceiling and laid sukka covering over the bed, for the baby's sake. Mar Zutra cites this as proof that Shammai's school acted on its own rulings. The Gemara answers that it proves nothing: anyone watching would think he did it only to let in more air.
why: The Gemara is asking whether Beit Shammai actually put their rulings into practice where they differed from Beit Hillel. This incident is offered as evidence that they did, and the Gemara deflects it.

people.name: Shammai the Elder
people.about: Makes a sukka over the bed of his newborn grandson.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: Cites the incident as an objection in the discussion.

terms.meaning: The temporary booth Jews dwell in during the festival of Sukkot. Its roof must be made of plant covering, not plaster.
The school of the Sage Shammai, which often disagreed with the school of Hillel (Beit Hillel). The law usually follows Beit Hillel.

note: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok recalled studying with Rabbi Yohanan the Horani and seeing him eat dry bread with salt in years of drought. He told his father, who had him bring olives. Rabbi Yohanan saw they were moist and said only, I do not eat olives; the translation explains he feared they had become ritually impure. Told again, the father sent word that the barrel had been pierced but the hole was clogged by sediment, a case even Beit Hillel rule pure. Though Rabbi Yohanan was a disciple of Shammai, he always acted by Beit Hillel's rulings.
why: The Gemara is gathering evidence on whether Beit Shammai acted on their own rulings. It argues that praising Rabbi Yohanan for following Beit Hillel makes sense only if Shammai's disciples normally followed Shammai.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
people.about: Tells the story of his teacher; carries the olives and messages between him and his father.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan the Ḥorani
people.about: Rabbi Elazar's teacher, a disciple of Shammai who acted by Beit Hillel's rulings.

terms.meaning: A state, under biblical law, that forbids certain foods to those who keep strict purity. Food can become liable to it once moistened by certain liquids.
The schools of the Sages Shammai and Hillel, which disagreed on many laws, including whether olive juice makes olives liable to impurity.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

note: A ruling permitting the rival wife of a daughter was said in the name of Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas, a great but very old Sage who could no longer come to the study hall. Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva went to him. He seated each on a golden couch, blessing the young Elazar and greeting Akiva as famous. When they asked, he said the law follows Beit Hillel; the ruling came from his younger brother Yonatan, a sharp disciple of Shammai, the firstborn of the Satan. He swore that the prophet Haggai, sitting on that very mortar, had forbidden the rival wife. Leaving, Akiva met Yonatan and withstood all his objections; Yonatan sneered that he was not yet even a cattle herder, and Akiva answered: not even a shepherd.
why: The Gemara had quoted only the opening line, as evidence that Beit Shammai's view was once followed in practice; here it tells the whole incident. Afterward it explains Haggai's other two rulings.

people.name: Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas
people.about: A great, aged Sage with dimmed eyes; the ruling was wrongly credited to him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Volunteers to go to Rabbi Dosa and introduces his companions.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Son of Rabbi Dosa's colleague Azarya; Rabbi Dosa blesses him with a verse.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Famous Sage; withstands Yonatan's objections and answers his insult humbly.

people.name: Yonatan
people.about: Rabbi Dosa's younger brother, a disciple of Shammai, who permitted the rival wife.

terms.meaning: When a man dies childless, his brother normally marries a widow. If one widow is that brother's own daughter she is forbidden to him; the question is whether her co-wife is also freed. Beit Shammai permit her to the brothers.
The schools of the Sages Shammai and Hillel, which disagreed on many laws. The law usually follows Beit Hillel.
An insult-compliment: someone extremely sharp and brazen in argument.

note: Rav Hisda recalled hearing from a great man, Rabbi Ami, that the Sages forbade a daughter-in-law only because of a daughter-in-law, and not understanding it. Chaldean astrologers had told him he would be a teacher. He said to himself: if I become a great teacher, I will work it out on my own; if I become a teacher of children, I will ask the Sages who come to the synagogue. Now, he said, he had worked it out himself: a man's daughter's daughter-in-law was forbidden only because she could be confused with his son's daughter-in-law.
why: The Gemara is listing relatives forbidden by the Sages rather than by the Torah, and has just corrected one item on Rav's list to read his daughter's daughter-in-law. Rav Hisda's account supplies the reason for that prohibition.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Tells how he came to understand a teaching he heard from Rabbi Ami.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The great man whose short teaching Rav Hisda heard.

terms.meaning: Astrologers who foretold a person's future; here they predict Rav Hisda will become a teacher.
Relatives one may not marry. Some are forbidden by the Torah; the Sages added others so that people would not confuse them with the Torah's cases.

note: Rabbi Yehuda was told of an armed bandit who was being led out to be executed at the pass of Cappadocia. He told the people there: go and tell the wife of Shimon the Priest that I killed her husband as I entered Lod (some say: as he entered Lod). On that word, his wife was allowed to remarry. Rabbi Yehuda replied that this proved nothing, because the bandit had said: I was with his murderers.
why: The mishna lets a woman remarry on a witness who says I killed him, while Rabbi Yehuda accepts only we killed him, which Rav Yehuda reads as I was with his murderers. This teaching is the basis for that distinction; the Gemara then explains how a mere accomplice was executed.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who is told of the case and reads it his own way.

people.name: Shimon the Priest
people.about: The man the bandit said was killed; his wife was allowed to remarry.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.
A woman whose husband disappears may not remarry until his death is established; here the bandit's words were accepted as that evidence.

note: Ravin brought Rabbi Yohanan's teaching that a woman who waits ten years after her husband before marrying again can no longer bear children; Rav Nahman said this applies only if she did not intend to remarry. Rava told his wife, the daughter of Rav Hisda, that the Sages were gossiping about her, since, as the translation explains, she had borne him children after more than ten years without a husband. She answered: My mind was on you.
why: The Gemara has been discussing sexual relations that cannot lead to pregnancy; it moves to this teaching about when a woman can still conceive, and Rava's exchange shows Rav Nahman's limit on it.

people.name: Ravin
people.about: Brings Rabbi Yohanan's teaching from the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage whose teaching about ten years Ravin reports.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Limits the teaching to a woman who did not intend to remarry.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Tells his wife that the Sages are gossiping about her.

people.name: daughter of Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Rava's wife, who answers that her mind was on him.

note: A woman came to Rav Yosef and told him that she had waited ten years after her husband and still given birth. He told her: My daughter, do not cast aspersions on the words of the Sages. She then admitted to him that she had had relations with a gentile.
why: Rabbi Yohanan has taught that a woman who waits ten years after her husband before remarrying can no longer conceive. The woman's case looks like a challenge to that teaching, and her confession shows it is not one.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage the woman comes to, who defends the Sages' teaching.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew.

note: When Rav came to Dardeshir, he publicly announced: Who will be my wife for the day? Rav Nahman made the same announcement when he came to Shakhnetziv. The Gemara answers that Sages are different, since their names are famous and their children will always be known. It also explains how they could marry on arrival: they sent messengers ahead so the woman could count seven clean days, or else they only spent time alone with her, since, as the saying goes, one who has bread in his basket is not like one who has none.
why: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov has just taught that a man should not marry wives in two countries, lest his children meet and unknowingly marry each other. The Gemara cites these two Sages' conduct as a challenge to that teaching.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who, visiting Dardeshir, announced he was seeking a wife for his stay.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: A Sage who did the same when visiting Shakhnetziv.

terms.meaning: After possible menstrual bleeding, a woman counts seven days without bleeding and immerses in a ritual bath before marital relations are permitted.
Being alone together with a woman. Here the Gemara suggests the Sages married only for companionship, not relations.

note: Rabbi Aha, lord of the capital, and Rabbi Tanhum son of Rabbi Hiyya of Akko village ransomed captive women who had been brought from Armon to Tiberias. One of them had been made pregnant by a gentile. They came to Rabbi Ami to ask about the child, and he told them that Rabbi Yohanan, Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Hanina all say that the child of a gentile or a slave and a Jewish woman is a mamzer.
why: The Gemara is debating the status of a child born to a Jewish woman and a gentile or slave. Rav Yosef then answers that counting names proves nothing, and lists Sages who rule such a child of unflawed lineage.

people.name: Rabbi Aḥa
people.about: Called lord of the capital; one of the two who ransomed the captives.

people.name: Rabbi Tanḥum
people.about: Son of Rabbi Hiyya, of Akko village; the other ransomer.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The Sage they ask, who cites three Sages' ruling.

terms.meaning: A child born of a forbidden union, barred from marrying most Jews. The question is whether a gentile father makes a child a mamzer.
Paid ransom to free Jews taken captive, a high duty in Jewish law.

note: A man came to Rav and asked about the child of a gentile or slave and a Jewish woman. Rav said the child's lineage is unflawed. The man, himself such a child, said: then give me your daughter. Rav refused. His grandson Shimi bar Hiyya quoted a saying about a camel that supposedly dances in Medes but does not when put to the test. Rav said that even if the man were like Joshua son of Nun he would not give him his daughter. Shimi answered that others would marry their daughters to a Joshua, but if Rav refused this man, no one would. The man would not leave and kept pleading. Rav set his eyes on him, and he died.
why: Abaye has argued that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permits such a child to marry within Israel. The Gemara brings this incident to show Rav ruled the same way, then lists other Sages who did too.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rules the child's lineage unflawed but refuses to give the man his daughter.

people.name: Shimi bar Ḥiyya
people.about: Rav's grandson, who challenges Rav's refusal.

terms.meaning: A small measure of volume. The proverb's camel dances on a space holding a single kav.
Free of any bar on marrying within the Jewish community.

note: Beloreya was a woman converting to Judaism. Her slaves immersed before she did, and the case came before the Sages, who ruled that the slaves had acquired themselves and were free.
why: Rav has ruled that a slave bought from a gentile who immerses for conversion before his new Jewish owner immerses him goes free. Rav Hisda infers from this case that had they immersed after her they would not have gone free, and raises it as a challenge; Rava answers it.

people.name: Beloreya
people.about: A convert whose slaves immersed before her.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Raises the incident as an objection in the discussion.

terms.meaning: Immersion in a ritual bath is a required step in converting to Judaism, and also in a gentile slave entering a Jewish owner's service.
A person who has formally joined the Jewish people.

note: When Rav Ashi wanted to immerse his slave Minyamin, he handed him over to Ravina and Rav Aha son of Rava and told them he would hold them responsible for him. They put a bridle on Minyamin's neck; at the moment of immersion they loosened it, and then tightened it again.
why: Shmuel has just said an owner must hold his slave firmly in the water, so that the immersion counts as entering slavery rather than conversion to freedom. This incident shows how it was done; the Gemara then explains each step.

people.name: Minyamin
people.about: Rav Ashi's slave, who is being immersed.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Minyamin's owner, who hands him to two Sages for the immersion.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: One of the two Sages who perform the immersion.

people.name: Rav Aḥa, son of Rava
people.about: The other Sage who performs the immersion.

terms.meaning: A gentile slave acquired by a Jew is immersed in a ritual bath. If the slave declares it is for conversion as a free man, he goes free.
A strap placed on the slave's neck to show the owner's control during the immersion.

flag: The STORY stops mid-incident: the next segment (the bucket of clay placed on Minyamin's head after immersion) belongs to the same incident.

note: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba came to Gavla. He saw Jewish women pregnant by converts who had been circumcised but not immersed, Jews drinking their wine that gentiles had poured, and Jews eating lupines that gentiles had cooked, and he said nothing to them. When he came to Rabbi Yohanan, Rabbi Yohanan told him to go and declare their children mamzerim, their wine forbidden as libation wine, and their lupines forbidden as food cooked by gentiles, because they were not learned in Torah.
why: The Gemara has been discussing immersion as the step that completes a conversion. Afterward it shows Rabbi Yohanan's ruling follows his own views: no one is a convert until circumcised and immersed, and a gentile's child with a Jewish woman is a mamzer.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba
people.about: Visits Gavla, sees lax practice and says nothing, then reports it.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Tells him to make public declarations against these practices.

terms.meaning: Plural of mamzer: a child of a forbidden union, barred from marrying most Jews.
Wine poured as an offering to idols, forbidden to Jews. The Sages extended the ban to wine handled by gentiles.
A rabbinic ban on certain foods cooked by non-Jews, even if the ingredients are permitted.
Bitter beans that must be cooked before eating.

note: Rabba told of an incident in the house of Rabbi Hiyya bar Rabbi. In Rav Yosef's version Rabbi Oshaya bar Rabbi was also there, and in Rav Safra's version Rabbi Oshaya son of Rabbi Hiyya as well. A convert came who had been circumcised but not yet immersed, and he was told: stay here until tomorrow, and we will immerse you.
why: The Gemara has been debating whether circumcision or immersion completes a conversion. Rabba then draws three rules from this incident: a conversion needs a court of three, it needs both circumcision and immersion, and a convert is not immersed at night.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Reports the incident and draws rules from it.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Rabbi
people.about: In whose house the convert came.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya bar Rabbi
people.about: Present, in the version Rav Yosef teaches.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya, son of Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Also present, in the version Rav Safra teaches.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Teaches the version with three Sages present.

terms.meaning: A person joining the Jewish people. For a man this requires circumcision and immersion in a ritual bath.
Dip fully in a ritual bath, the final step of conversion.

note: A man everyone took to be Jewish came to Rabbi Yehuda and said he had converted in private, so he was not really Jewish. Rabbi Yehuda asked whether he had witnesses; he had none. He asked whether he had children; he did. Rabbi Yehuda told him he was believed about himself, and so could disqualify himself from marrying a Jewish woman, but he was not believed when it came to disqualifying his children.
why: Rabbi Yehuda has just ruled that a conversion done in private, without a court, is not valid. The Gemara then asks how his ruling here fits his other teaching that a father is believed about his children's status, and offers two explanations.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who held that a conversion done privately, outside a court, is not valid; the man brings his claim to him.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew who formally joins the Jewish people. Rabbi Yehuda held this had to be done before a court to count.

note: Three Sages, Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha, were sitting in Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha's courtyard and talking. They recalled a city in the Land of Israel whose slaves refused to be circumcised. The masters put up with them for twelve months and then sold them to gentiles. The Sages asked whose opinion the townspeople had followed; the story itself does not give the answer.
why: The discussion is about when a Jewish master may keep an uncircumcised slave. The Gemara answers the Sages' question with a teaching that a master may wait up to twelve months before selling such a slave to gentiles.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappi
people.about: One of the three Sages talking in the courtyard.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: One of the three Sages talking in the courtyard.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa
people.about: One of the three Sages; the conversation takes place in his courtyard.

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel.
Non-Jews.

note: Rav Dimi brought a report from the Land of Israel: a girl in the village of Hitlu was sweeping the house when a village dog sodomized her from behind. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled she was still permitted to marry a priest. Shmuel added that she was permitted even to a High Priest. The Gemara objects that there was no High Priest in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's day, and explains that Shmuel meant she would be fit for one.
why: Rabbi Shimi bar Hiyya has just ruled that a woman who had intercourse with an animal is not considered a harlot and may marry a priest; this case is the precedent. The Gemara then asks for the verse showing there is no harlotry with an animal.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who brought this report when he came from the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who ruled the girl could still marry a priest.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who added that she was fit even for a High Priest.

terms.meaning: Here, marriage to a priest (kohen). Priests may not marry a woman considered a harlot, and a High Priest must marry a virgin.
The chief priest who served in the Temple; there was none after the Temple was destroyed.

note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi told of a city in the Land of Israel where a family's lineage was challenged. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sent Rabbi Romanus to investigate. He found that the family included a woman who had converted before she was three years and a day old and had married a priest, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled she was permitted to the priesthood. When Rabbi Zeira asked whether he had drawn his ruling from this case, Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi said he had heard it from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explicitly.
why: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi had reported that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules like Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai, who permits a girl converted before age three to marry a priest. Rabbi Zeira wanted to know whether this was said outright or only inferred from this case.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage who reported the case.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who sent an investigator and permitted the woman to the priesthood.

people.name: Rabbi Romanus
people.about: The Sage sent to examine the family's lineage.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi
people.about: Transmitted Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling and insists he heard it directly.

terms.meaning: The age below which, in Talmudic law, intercourse does not count as removing a girl's virginity. A girl converted before then could be treated as never having had relations as a gentile.

note: A priest married a woman who had converted before she was three years and a day old. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak challenged him. The priest answered that Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi had reported, in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's name, that the law follows Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai, who permits such a marriage. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak told him to divorce her, and said that otherwise he would remove Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi from his ear.
why: The Gemara has just shown that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules like Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai on such a convert marrying a priest. This case shows a Sage refusing to rely on that ruling in practice.

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: The Sage who ordered the priest to divorce his wife.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi
people.about: The Sage whose report the priest relied on.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage in whose name the ruling was reported.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai
people.about: The Sage whose opinion the priest claimed to follow.

terms.meaning: A kohen, a descendant of Aaron. Priests are barred from certain marriages, including, in the view of most Sages, to a woman who converted.
Jewish law; the binding ruling.

note: Yehoshua ben Gamla, a priest, betrothed Marta bat Baitos, a widow. The king then appointed him High Priest, and he went ahead and married her. Rav Yosef saw a conspiracy in the wording that the king appointed him, and cited Rav Asi: Marta bat Baitos brought King Yannai a vessel full of dinars until he made Yehoshua ben Gamla High Priest.
why: The mishna rules that a priest who betrothed a widow and was then appointed High Priest may still marry her, and cites this marriage as the example. The Gemara then reads the wording closely and finds that the appointment was bought.

people.name: Yehoshua ben Gamla
people.about: A priest who betrothed a widow and was then made High Priest.

people.name: Marta bat Baitos
people.about: The widow he betrothed; Rav Asi says she paid the king to appoint him.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: The king who made Yehoshua ben Gamla High Priest.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who saw a conspiracy behind the appointment.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The Sage who reported the payment to the king.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage, which already makes the couple legally bound; the wedding itself comes later.
The chief priest of the Temple. The Torah forbids him to marry a widow.
The brother of a man who died childless; he is obligated to marry the widow (levirate marriage) or release her.
A measure of volume, half a se'a, used here for the size of a vessel full of coins.

note: Rabbi Akiva taught that one who had students in his youth should have more in his old age. The Gemara illustrates: he had twelve thousand pairs of students from Gevat to Antipatris, and all of them died in one period because they did not treat each other with respect. The world was desolate of Torah until he went to the Sages in the South and taught five new students, Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua, who upheld the Torah. It is taught that the first students all died between Passover and Shavuot, a bad death, which Rav Nahman says was diphtheria.
why: The Gemara is discussing whether a man who already has children should have more. Rabbi Yehoshua reads a verse from Ecclesiastes to say yes, and Rabbi Akiva reads the same verse about students, which his own life illustrates.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A great teacher whose first twelve thousand pairs of students died; he then taught five new ones.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: One of Rabbi Akiva's later students who upheld the Torah.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: One of Rabbi Akiva's later students.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: One of Rabbi Akiva's later students.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Identifies the bad death the students died as diphtheria.

terms.meaning: The festival seven weeks after Passover.
A throat infection that can choke a person to death.

note: Rabbi Elazar taught that all craftsmen will one day work the land, and that no occupation is lowlier than farming. Seeing a field that had been plowed across its width, he said to the field that even if it were plowed lengthwise as well, doing business was better than farming it.
why: The Gemara is stringing together sayings of Rabbi Elazar; this one leads into more sayings comparing trade with farming, from Rav, Rava and Rav Pappa.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who speaks to a plowed field about how little farming pays.

flag: Mostly sayings; the only event is Rabbi Elazar's one remark to a field.

note: When Rav took leave of his teacher Rabbi Hiyya, Rabbi Hiyya blessed him that God should save him from something worse than death. Rav searched and found the verse "I find more bitter than death the woman." Indeed, Rav's wife tormented him: if he asked for lentils she made peas, and if he asked for peas she made lentils. When their son Hiyya grew up, he passed on his father's requests reversed, so Rav got what he wanted. Rav praised the trick, but told his son to stop, since it meant speaking lies.
why: The Gemara is collecting sayings and stories about wives, good and bad; this one is followed by Rabbi Hiyya's own troubled marriage and more teachings on a bad wife.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A student of Rabbi Hiyya whose wife did the opposite of whatever he asked.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Rav's uncle and teacher, who blessed him on parting.

people.name: Ḥiyya
people.about: Rav's son, who reversed his father's requests to his mother.

terms.meaning: A name for God.

note: Rabbi Hiyya's wife tormented him, yet whenever he found something she would like, he wrapped it in his shawl and brought it to her. Rav asked why, since she tormented him. Rabbi Hiyya answered that it is enough that wives raise our children and save us from sin. Separately, Rav Yehuda was teaching his son Rav Yitzhak the verse "I find more bitter than death the woman"; asked for an example, he said: your mother. The Gemara notes he had also named her as an example of finding peace with one's first wife, and explains that she was forceful but easily calmed.
why: The Gemara is gathering stories and sayings about wives, and goes on to define a bad wife and what a husband may do about one.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: A Sage whose wife tormented him, yet he brought her gifts.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's student, who asks him why he is kind to her.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage teaching his son, who names the boy's mother in two opposite verses.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak
people.about: Rav Yehuda's son.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

flag: Combines two separate anecdotes (Rabbi Hiyya's wife; Rav Yehuda and his son) and begins mid-sentence across a page break.

note: Rabbi Yohanan reported a case of four sisters in Tzippori. The first circumcised her son and he died, the second circumcised hers and he died, and the third circumcised hers and he died. The fourth came before Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who told her: do not circumcise.
why: The Gemara is asking whether, for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, a pattern is set by two events or three. This case seems to show three, but the Gemara replies that the third sister may simply never have asked him, and that the case teaches that sisters together can set a pattern.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who told the fourth sister not to circumcise her son.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Reported the case, through Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba
people.about: Passed on Rabbi Yohanan's report.

terms.meaning: In Talmudic law, a pattern repeated enough times that it is assumed to continue; here, that a family's sons die from circumcision.

note: Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef came from the Land of Israel and reported a case brought before Rabbi Yohanan in the synagogue of Maon on a Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbat. One sister had circumcised her son and he died, and a second sister had circumcised hers and he died. When the third sister came before him, Rabbi Yohanan told her: go and circumcise.
why: The Gemara asks what the final ruling is: does a pattern of deaths start after two cases or three? This report is its answer, three. Abaye warns Rav Yitzhak to be sure of his report, since it permits something forbidden and dangerous.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef
people.about: A Sage who brought this report from the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage who told the third sister to circumcise her son.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, the holiest fast day of the Jewish year.
The Sabbath. A circumcision done on the eighth day is performed even on Shabbat.

note: Relying on Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef's report, Abaye married Huma, daughter of Isi. Huma had been married to Rahava of Pumbedita, who died, and then to Rav Yitzhak son of Rabba bar bar Hana, who also died. Abaye married her, and he died too.
why: Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef had reported that a pattern is set only after three cases, so a woman widowed twice could remarry. Rava then criticizes Abaye: he himself had called that reporter unreliable, and a rule about circumcision need not apply to marriage.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who married a twice-widowed woman and died.

people.name: Ḥuma
people.about: Daughter of Isi; her first two husbands died, and then Abaye.

people.name: Raḥava of Pumbedita
people.about: Huma's first husband, who died.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak, son of Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: Huma's second husband, who died.

note: A woman came before Rav Nahman wanting a divorce because her husband could not father children. He told her she was not commanded to have children. She asked whether a woman like her does not need a staff for her hand and a hoe for her burial, and Rav Nahman said that in such a case the husband is forced to divorce her. Separately, Rabbi Hiyya's wife Yehudit suffered terribly giving birth to twins. In disguise she asked him whether a woman is commanded to have children; he said no, and she drank a potion to make herself infertile. When he found out, he said he wished she had borne him one more set of twins, since their sons Yehuda and Hizkiyya and daughters Pazi and Tavi were twins.
why: The Gemara is asking whether a woman is commanded to have children, which decides whether she can demand a divorce from a husband who cannot father them. Both stories assume she is not, and the Gemara next tests that with a case that seems to show the opposite.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: A Sage who forced a husband to divorce his wife so she could have children to care for her.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: A Sage whose wife asked him, in disguise, whether women must have children.

people.name: Yehudit
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's wife, who drank an infertility potion after painful births.

people.name: Yehuda and Ḥizkiyya
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's twin sons.

people.name: Pazi and Tavi
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's twin daughters.

terms.meaning: The commandment to have children. The Sages here hold that it falls on men, not women.
The ketuba, which sets the money a wife receives if she is divorced or widowed.

flag: Combines two separate stories: the woman before Rav Nahman, and Rabbi Hiyya's wife Yehudit.

note: Rabbi Yitzhak reported a case of a woman who was half slave and half free, so she could marry neither a slave nor a free Jew. The court forced her master to set her free. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak explained that this was because men were treating her as ownerless, so she was falling into promiscuity.
why: The Gemara had said women are not commanded to have children. This case seems to show they are, since her master was forced to free her so she could marry; Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak answers that she was freed to stop the sexual misconduct.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak
people.about: Reported the case, through Rav Aha bar Rav Ketina.

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: Explains why the court forced the master to free her.

terms.meaning: A status that arises when a slave owned by two partners is freed by only one; such a person can lawfully marry neither a slave nor a free Jew.

note: A woman brought a fine wool robe into her marriage, listed in her marriage contract. When her husband died, his children took the robe and spread it over his body as a shroud, and she wanted it back. Rava ruled that the dead man had acquired it. Nanai son of Rav Yosef son of Rava objected to Rav Kahana that Rava himself had said the law follows Rav Yehuda, who lets a wife take back such items. Rav Kahana answered that even Rav Yehuda agrees the robe stays in the husband's possession until she collects it.
why: The discussion is about who owns property a wife brings into marriage at a fixed value: Rav Yehuda says she may take it back as a family heirloom. This case tests that view, and the Gemara links Rava's ruling to his rule that consecrating something frees it from a debt claim.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled the dead man had acquired the robe.

people.name: Nanai, son of Rav Yosef, son of Rava
people.about: Challenged Rava's ruling in a question to Rav Kahana.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Answered the challenge.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage whose ruling on a wife's property is debated.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, which lists what a wife brought into the marriage and what she receives if widowed or divorced.
Anything set aside for a corpse, like a shroud, may no longer be used for any benefit.

note: Rabbi Yohanan was sitting and teaching that leftover sacrificial meat burned at its proper time must be burned by day, but otherwise may be burned by day or night. Rabbi Elazar challenged him with a teaching that a late circumcision must also be done by day, drawn from the word "and" in the verse, and Rabbi Yohanan was silent. After Rabbi Elazar left, Rabbi Yohanan told Reish Lakish he had seen ben Pedat expounding like Moses from the mouth of God. Reish Lakish said it was not his own idea but a baraita in Torat Kohanim. Rabbi Yohanan went out and learned that whole work in three days, and understood it fully in three months.
why: The Gemara has explained that two early Sages disagree over whether the word "and" in a verse makes a late circumcision a daytime-only act. This episode shows Rabbi Yohanan holding the same view about leftover sacrificial meat, and being challenged on it.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A great Sage who was silenced by his student's challenge and then mastered the source.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat, who challenged Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Rabbi Yohanan's colleague, who pointed out the source of the challenge.

people.name: Moses
people.about: Named in Rabbi Yohanan's praise of Rabbi Elazar's teaching.

terms.meaning: Meat of a sacrifice left past the time it may be eaten; it must be burned.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
An early collection of teachings on the book of Leviticus, also called the Sifra.
The Hebrew letter that means "and"; some Sages draw extra rules from it when it seems unneeded.

note: A man was climbing a palm tree when a thorn pierced his testicles, and a discharge like a thread of pus came out of him. Later he had children. Shmuel sent the case to Rav, who told him to go and find out where the man's children came from.
why: The discussion asks whether a man whose testicles were pierced counts as having crushed testicles, a condition that bars him from marrying into the community. The case seems to show such a man can father children, but Rav's reply suggests the children were not his.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who sent the case to Rav.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who doubted the children were the man's own.

terms.meaning: An injury the Torah lists as barring a man from marrying a Jewish woman by birth ("entering the congregation").

note: In Mata Mehasya a man's member had been cut like an open gutter; Mar bar Rav Ashi trimmed it into the shape of a quill and declared him fit. In Pumbedita a man's seminal duct became blocked and he emitted semen through the urinary duct. Rav Beivai bar Abaye wanted to declare him fit. Rav Pappi mocked him, saying that coming from a short-lived family he spoke short-lived words, since semen that does not pass through its proper place does not fertilize.
why: The discussion is about which injuries to the genitals bar a man from marrying into the community. Rav Pappa has just ruled that a cut shaped like a quill or a gutter is fit, and these cases apply that ruling and test where it stops.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Reshaped an injured man's member and declared him fit.

people.name: Rav Beivai bar Abaye
people.about: Wanted to declare the Pumbedita man fit.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: Mocked Rav Beivai's ruling and held the man unfit.

terms.meaning: Permitted to marry a Jewish woman by birth ("enter the congregation"), despite the injury.
Rav Pappi's insult: Rav Beivai's family was descended from the priest Eli, whose descendants were cursed to die young.

flag: The last segment (Shmuel's ruling on a punctured member, and Rava's discussion of it) is a legal ruling, not part of the two incidents.

note: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda came from the Land of Israel and reported that Rabbi Zakkai once recited a teaching before Rabbi Yohanan: an Ammonite woman is fit, her son by an Ammonite is unfit, her daughter by an Ammonite is fit, and if the father had not converted, the daughter is unfit. Rabbi Yohanan told him to go and teach it outside, and began explaining that its first parts were too obvious to need teaching. The rest of his answer comes after the story ends.
why: Rabbi Yohanan has just been cited as permitting the daughter of an Ammonite convert and a Jewish woman to marry a priest. This teaching says she is unfit, so he rejects it as unreliable.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: Brought this report from the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Heard the teaching and rejected it.

terms.meaning: A member of a neighboring nation. The Torah bars Ammonite men, even after converting, from marrying into Israel, but not Ammonite women.

terms.term: Go out and teach it outside
terms.meaning: A way of saying a teaching is unreliable and should not be studied in the study hall.

flag: Rabbi Yohanan's reply is cut off: his explanation of why he rejects the teaching continues after the story ends.

note: Rabbi Yehuda recalls his friend Minyamin, an Egyptian convert who studied with Rabbi Akiva. Minyamin said that he, a first-generation Egyptian convert, had married another first-generation Egyptian convert, and that he planned to marry off his son to a second-generation Egyptian convert so that his grandson would be allowed to enter the congregation. The Gemara adds that Rabbi Yohanan told the teacher reciting this account to change it: Minyamin meant to marry his son to a first-generation convert.
why: The Gemara is asking whether a child's generation is counted from the father or the mother. Rava uses Minyamin's plan to challenge the view, credited to Rabbi Yohanan, that the father decides; the corrected wording answers him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who reports what his friend Minyamin told him.

people.name: Minyamin
people.about: An Egyptian convert, a friend of Rabbi Yehuda and a student of Rabbi Akiva, planning whom his son should marry.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who cites this account as an objection.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who told the reciter to correct the wording of the account.

terms.meaning: The Torah says Egyptians who join the Jewish people may marry into the community only from the third generation. A first- or second-generation Egyptian convert may not marry a born Jew.
To be allowed to marry a born Jew.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
Here, a person whose job was to memorize and recite early teachings word for word.

note: A man living in Rabbi Ami's neighborhood was publicly declared by Rabbi Ami to be a mamzer. The man went about weeping. Rabbi Ami told him: I have given you life.
why: The Gemara has just quoted Rav Yehuda that a mamzer who is publicly known survives, while one who is not known dies at the hand of Heaven. Rabbi Ami's words to the weeping man apply that teaching.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: A Sage who declared his neighbor a mamzer and then told him he had been given life.

terms.meaning: A child born of a forbidden union, such as adultery or incest. A mamzer may not marry a born Jew, and the status passes to his descendants.

note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recalls going to learn Torah from Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua. The students there ganged up on him like the fighting roosters of Beit Bukya and would not let him study. He managed to learn only one thing: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that a man who has intercourse with a hermaphrodite is liable to stoning, as if with a male.
why: The mishna quotes Rabbi Eliezer's ruling about a hermaphrodite, and the Gemara has just shown that Rabbi Eliezer does not treat a hermaphrodite as a full male. This memory of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi confirms the wording of that ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: A Sage, called simply Rabbi, who tells of his attempt to study with Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua
people.about: The teacher whose students would not let Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi learn.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage whose ruling on a hermaphrodite was the one thing Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi learned there.

terms.meaning: A person with both male and female sexual organs, whose legal status the Sages debate.
The severest form of court execution in Jewish law, prescribed for certain forbidden sexual acts, including relations between males.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

note: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, a priest, used to collect first tithe from a certain garden. Rabbi Akiva went and moved the garden's entrance so that it faced the cemetery, where a priest may not go. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya said: Akiva comes with his satchel, and I have to live?
why: The Gemara has just set out the dispute: Rabbi Akiva holds the first tithe belongs only to Levites, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya that a priest may receive it too. This episode shows each acting on his view; afterwards the Gemara asks why Rabbi Akiva blocked the entrance.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: A priest who held that priests may receive the first tithe, and collected it from this garden.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who held the first tithe goes only to Levites, and moved the garden's entrance.

terms.meaning: A tenth of produce that the Torah gives to the Levites, the tribe that served in the Temple.
A descendant of Aaron. Priests may not become impure through contact with the dead, so they may not enter a cemetery.

note: Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov says he heard that a court may flog and punish beyond what the Torah requires, not to break the Torah but to build a fence around it. His example: in the days of the Greeks, a man rode a horse on Shabbat. He was brought to court and stoned, not because he deserved it, but because the times required it.
why: The Gemara is asking whether the Sages have the power to uproot a Torah law. This report of a court executing a man for an act the Torah does not punish by death is brought as evidence that they can.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov
people.about: A Sage who reports what he heard about a court's power to punish, with this incident as his example.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest. Riding a horse on Shabbat is forbidden by rabbinic law, not by the Torah itself.
Executed by stoning, the severest form of court execution, which the Torah sets for serious Shabbat violations.
The period of Greek rule over the Land of Israel.

note: A man had relations with his own wife under a fig tree, in public view. He was brought to court and flogged, not because he deserved it, but because the times required it.
why: The Gemara is asking whether the Sages can uproot a Torah law by an active deed. This second precedent, after the man stoned for riding on Shabbat, seems to say they can; the Gemara limits it to safeguarding the Torah.

terms.meaning: Given lashes, a punishment a court could impose.

note: Rabbi Yannai's sharecropper used to bring him a basket of fruit every Friday. One Friday he was late, so Rabbi Yannai set aside tithe from fruit in his house on behalf of the fruit not yet delivered, and then asked Rabbi Hiyya whether this worked. Rabbi Hiyya told him he had acted well, citing a verse about tithing on Shabbat. Rabbi Yannai said he had dreamed the words "bruised reed" and feared it meant he had leaned on something weak. Rabbi Hiyya answered that the dream meant a different verse: "A bruised reed he shall not break."
why: The Gemara is listing Sages who hold that a person can act on something that does not yet exist or is not yet his. This episode is its proof that Rabbi Yannai, like Rabbi Hiyya, holds that view.

people.name: Rabbi Yannai
people.about: A Sage who owned land worked by a sharecropper and tithed fruit that had not yet arrived.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The Sage Rabbi Yannai consulted, who approved what he had done and read his dream.

terms.meaning: A tenant farmer who works someone else's land and pays the owner with part of the crop.
A portion of produce that must be set aside before it may be eaten. It may not be set aside on Shabbat.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

note: A man had relations with his mother-in-law. Rav Yehuda had him brought and flogged. Rav Yehuda told him: If Shmuel had not said that the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda, I would make your wife forbidden to you for ever.
why: Rabbi Yehuda holds that a man who sleeps with his mother-in-law becomes forbidden to his wife, and Shmuel ruled against him. This case shows Rav Yehuda following Shmuel's ruling in practice.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who judged the man and reported Shmuel's ruling.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Rav Yehuda's teacher, who ruled that the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: An earlier Sage who held that such a man is forbidden to his wife.

terms.meaning: Jewish law; the binding ruling on a question.

note: Rabbi Elazar taught a ruling in the study hall without saying he had it from his teacher Rabbi Yohanan, and Rabbi Yohanan was angry. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi tried to calm him by recalling how Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei once argued so fiercely in the synagogue of Tiberias that a Torah scroll was torn, and Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma predicted that the synagogue would become a place of idol worship, as it did. That made Rabbi Yohanan angrier: were they now making his student his colleague? Then Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi pointed out that Joshua taught without saying "Moses told me," yet everyone knew it was Moses' Torah; so too everyone knows Rabbi Elazar's teaching is Rabbi Yohanan's. Rabbi Yohanan was calmed.
why: The ruling Rabbi Elazar repeated is the one just discussed, about a minor's relations with his yevama. The Gemara then explains Rabbi Yohanan's anger: a Sage quoted by name in this world, his lips move in the grave.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The teacher who was angered that his ruling was taught without his name.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Rabbi Yohanan's student, who taught the ruling without naming him.

people.name: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
people.about: Sages who tried to calm Rabbi Yohanan and made him angrier.

people.name: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi
people.about: The Sage who succeeded in calming Rabbi Yohanan; Rabbi Yohanan later praised him.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma
people.about: A Sage present at the argument in Tiberias who predicted the synagogue's fate.

terms.meaning: The house of learning where the Sages taught and debated.
The handwritten parchment scroll of the Five Books of Moses, treated with great reverence.
Jewish law; here, a specific legal ruling.

note: Rabbi Yosei reports a case: Niftayim, a convert, married the wife of his brother from the same mother. The case came before the Sages, who said that a convert has no marriage. The Gemara objects that a convert's marriage is surely valid, and rereads the ruling to mean that the ban on a brother's wife does not apply to a convert.
why: Rav Aha bar Yaakov and Rav Sheshet disagree over a convert and his maternal brother's wife. This case is offered as proof that it is permitted even if the brother married her after converting; the Gemara answers that he married her before.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who reports the case.

people.name: Niftayim
people.about: A convert who married the wife of his brother from the same mother.

terms.meaning: A person who has joined the Jewish people. In Jewish law a convert is like a newborn, so earlier family ties may not count.
The Torah forbids a man to marry his brother's wife, apart from the special case of levirate marriage.

note: Ben Yasiyan traveled to cities overseas and found a convert married to the wife of his brother from the same mother. He asked: My son, who allowed you this? The convert pointed to a woman and her seven sons and said that on this very bench Rabbi Akiva sat and taught two things: a convert may marry his maternal brother's wife, and God spoke to Jonah only twice, not a third time.
why: The Gemara is asking whether a convert may marry his maternal brother's wife even when the brother married her after converting. This account is offered as proof; the Gemara answers that the brother married her before converting, then asks whether the convert can be trusted.

people.name: Ben Yasiyan
people.about: A Sage who met the convert on his travels and questioned him.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage who, according to the convert, permitted this marriage.

people.name: Jonah
people.about: The biblical prophet, mentioned in the second teaching of Rabbi Akiva.

terms.meaning: A person who has joined the Jewish people. In Jewish law a convert is like a newborn, so earlier family ties may not count.
God's presence as it reveals itself to people, here in speaking to a prophet.
Coastal cities beyond the Land of Israel.

note: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok said that in all his life he testified only once, and on his word a slave was promoted to the status of a priest. The Gemara objects that God would not let the righteous cause such a mistake, so he must mean that they almost promoted the slave. It explains how: he had seen the man receive teruma in Rabbi Yosei's town, then testified about it in Rabbi Yehuda's town, where receiving teruma was taken as proof that a man is a priest.
why: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei disagree on whether teruma may be handed to a priest's slave without his master, because in Rabbi Yehuda's town receiving teruma was taken as proof of priestly lineage. This account shows what that local difference could lead to.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
people.about: A Sage whose one testimony nearly led to a slave being treated as a priest.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage in whose town teruma was handed to a priest's slave, without this proving lineage.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage in whose town receiving teruma was treated as proof of being a priest.

terms.meaning: A portion of produce given to priests, which only priests and their households may eat.
Granted the presumed status of a priest, with its privileges and restrictions, on the strength of evidence such as testimony.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

note: Rav Ashi came to Rav Kahana's house, and Rav Kahana asked him to come up and make a fifth judge for a halitza. Rav Kahana recalled that Rav Yehuda once told him to go up to the bundle of reeds and join the five. When people asked Rav Yehuda why five were needed, he said it was to make the matter public.
why: The Gemara has ruled that halitza needs only three judges, and that it takes place at a set location. These cases of five judges at a fixed spot explain why the Sages sometimes used more: to publicize it, not because the law requires it.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage visiting Rav Kahana, who was asked to make up the five.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage who invited Rav Ashi to join and recalled an earlier case with Rav Yehuda.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rav Kahana's teacher, who used five judges for halitza to make it public.

terms.meaning: The ceremony that releases a childless widow from marrying her late husband's brother. She removes his shoe and spits before a court, and is then free to marry anyone.
A spot marked by a bundle of reeds, set aside as the regular place where the court met for halitza.

note: Rav Yehuda asked Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda to go up to the bundle of reeds and make a fifth judge for a halitza, to make the matter public. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda answered that a halitza court must be made of born Israelites, not converts, and he was a convert. Rav Yehuda said he would take money from someone on the word of a man like Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda. The Gemara objects that the Torah needs two witnesses, and explains that he meant he would cancel a loan document on his word.
why: The discussion is about who may sit on a court for halitza. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's refusal leads the Gemara to Rava's rule on when a convert may judge, and to why a halitza judge needs two Jewish-born parents.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who asked his student to join the halitza court and then praised his honesty.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: A convert who declined to sit on the halitza court because he was a convert.

terms.meaning: The ceremony that releases a childless widow from marrying her late husband's brother. She removes his shoe and spits before a court, and is then free to marry anyone.
A spot marked by a bundle of reeds, set aside as the regular place where the court met for halitza.
A person who has joined the Jewish people rather than being born into it.
A written loan document that lets the lender collect the debt.

note: Rabbi Yosei tells of a trip to the city of Netzivin, where he met an Elder who knew Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira well; the Sage often ate at his table. Asked whether he had seen Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira conduct halitza, the Elder said many times. Asked whether with a soft shoe or a sandal, he replied: Does anyone perform halitza with a soft shoe? Rabbi Yosei asked him why, then, Rabbi Meir said halitza with a soft shoe is valid. Rabbi Yaakov reports in Rabbi Meir's name that it is allowed from the start.
why: The Gemara has been asking whether halitza may be done with a soft leather shoe from the start, or is only valid after the fact. It cites this account to show that early Sages disagreed on it, then asks the reason of those who forbid it.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who traveled to Netzivin and questioned an Elder there.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: A Sage of Netzivin who often ate at the Elder's table and conducted halitza with a sandal.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who ruled that halitza with a soft shoe is valid.

people.name: Rabbi Yaakov
people.about: A Sage who reports Rabbi Meir's view that a soft shoe may be used from the start.

terms.meaning: The ceremony that releases a childless widow from marrying her late husband's brother. She removes his shoe and spits before a court, and is then free to marry anyone.
A childless widow bound to her late husband's brother until he marries her or releases her through halitza.
From the start; doing something as the preferred way, rather than accepting it only after it has been done.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

note: Abaye was with his teacher Rav Yosef when a widow came to perform halitza. Rav Yosef told Abaye to give the brother his sandal, and Abaye gave him his left one. Rav Yosef objected that the Sages allowed a left shoe only after the fact. Abaye answered that the same goes for a shoe that is not the brother's own. Rav Yosef explained that he had meant: give him the sandal and transfer ownership of it to him.
why: The mishna says halitza is valid with a shoe that is not the brother's own, and the Sages read "his shoe" as one that fits him. This episode shows that using a borrowed or left shoe is still not the ideal way.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rav Yosef's student, who lent his left sandal for the halitza.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who was overseeing the halitza.

terms.meaning: The ceremony that releases a childless widow from marrying her late husband's brother. She removes his shoe and spits before a court, and is then free to marry anyone.
A childless widow bound to her late husband's brother until he marries her or releases her through halitza.
Accepted as valid once done, though it should not be done that way to begin with (ab initio).

note: A widow came before Rabbi Ami for halitza, with Rabbi Abba bar Memel sitting before him, and she spat before removing the shoe. Rabbi Ami said: let her remove the shoe and the case is done. Rabbi Abba objected that she must spit, and asked why she should not simply spit again. Rabbi Ami said that would be a disaster: people would think the first spitting meant nothing and come to let a released widow marry the brothers. When Rabbi Abba objected that the steps must be in order, Rabbi Ami said the order is not essential. Rabbi Abba thought he was just being brushed off, but he went out, checked, and found a teaching that either order is valid.
why: The Gemara is weighing a ruling sent to Shmuel's father: a widow who spat first need only remove the shoe and need not spit again. This case is cited as an instance of that ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The Sage overseeing the halitza, who ruled that she did not need to spit again.

people.name: Rabbi Abba bar Memel
people.about: A Sage sitting before Rabbi Ami who challenged his ruling, then confirmed it.

terms.meaning: The ceremony that releases a childless widow from marrying her late husband's brother. She removes his shoe and spits before a court, and is then free to marry anyone.
A childless widow bound to her late husband's brother until he marries her or releases her through halitza.
A widow who has already gone through halitza; she may no longer marry any of the brothers.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

note: Levi went out to the villages, and people asked him three questions: may a woman without arms perform halitza; is it valid if a widow spat blood; and does the verse about "the writing of truth" imply there is writing in Heaven that is not true? He had no answer, so he went and asked in the study hall. There he was told that the Torah does not say she must remove the shoe by hand, nor that she must spit saliva. On the verse, the answer was that a decree sealed with an oath can never be canceled, while one without an oath can.
why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Abba bar Memel checked a halitza ruling in the study hall. Levi's questions bring more halitza cases, and his third question leads into the discussion of a decree sealed with an oath, shown by the house of Eli.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who went to teach in the villages and brought their questions back to the study hall.

terms.meaning: The ceremony that releases a childless widow from marrying her late husband's brother. She removes his shoe and spits before a court, and is then free to marry anyone.
A childless widow bound to her late husband's brother until he marries her or releases her through halitza.
The house of learning where the Sages taught and debated.

note: Rabba taught that a descendant of the house of Eli cannot gain atonement through sacrifice, but can through Torah study. Abaye taught that he can through acts of kindness. Both were themselves from the house of Eli: Rabba, who devoted himself to Torah, lived forty years, and Abaye, who devoted himself to Torah and kindness, lived sixty.
why: Rabbi Yonatan has just shown from the oath against Eli's house that a sentence sealed with an oath cannot be torn up, even with offerings. Rabba and Abaye read that verse as leaving another way out.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage descended from the house of Eli who devoted himself to Torah and lived forty years.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage descended from the house of Eli who devoted himself to Torah and kindness and lived sixty years.

terms.meaning: The descendants of Eli, the priest at Shiloh in the Book of Samuel. God swore that their sin would not be atoned for by sacrifice, and that they would die young.
Good deeds done for others, such as helping the needy, visiting the sick and burying the dead.
Animal and grain offerings brought at the Temple, among other things to atone for sin.

note: A family in Jerusalem had members who kept dying at around eighteen years old. They came and told Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai. He said: perhaps you are from the family of Eli, of whom it is written that all their offspring shall die as young men; go and study Torah, and you will live. They went and studied Torah and lived, and people called them the family of Yohanan, after him.
why: The Gemara has just told how Rabba and Abaye, descendants of Eli, lived longer through Torah and kindness. This account from the Sages is a second example that Torah study can overcome the decree against Eli's house.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Sage the family turned to, who told them to study Torah.

terms.meaning: The descendants of Eli, the priest at Shiloh in the Book of Samuel. God swore that their sin would not be atoned for by sacrifice, and that they would die young.

note: Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi were debating whether one who prays should look down or up, each citing a verse. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, joined them and quoted his father: eyes down, heart up. When Rabbi entered the study hall, the heavy Rabbi Yishmael stepped over the heads of those seated, and Rabbi's attendant Abdon challenged him; the exchange ended with Yishmael asking, 'Is your teacher God?' When a yevama came, Rabbi sent Abdon to examine her, but Yishmael quoted his father that a minor may perform ḥalitza, so Rabbi called Abdon back. Yishmael rebuked him for stepping over heads again, and Rabbi told Abdon to stay where he was. At that moment Abdon was struck with leprosy, his two sons drowned, and their wives refused their marriages.
why: The Gemara asks who the Rabbis are who, against Rabbi Meir, let a female minor perform ḥalitza, and answers that it is Rabbi Yosei, as his son reports him in this incident.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Sits debating the direction of one's gaze in prayer with Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A very heavy Sage who quotes his father's rulings and clashes with Abdon.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, head of the study hall; Abdon is his student and attendant.

people.name: Abdon
people.about: Rabbi's student and attendant, who challenges Rabbi Yishmael and is then punished.

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: Comments that God shamed Abdon in this world, sparing him in the World-to-Come.

terms.meaning: The ceremony in which a childless widow removes the shoe of her late husband's brother, releasing both from the duty of levirate marriage so she may marry someone else.
A childless widow bound to her late husband's brother under the law of levirate marriage until he marries her or performs ḥalitza.
A girl married off as a minor could annul the marriage by declaring that she refuses her husband.

note: A widow was bound to her late husband's brother, but he was not suitable for her. The judges told him to let her perform ḥalitza on condition that she pay him two hundred dinars. The case later came before Rabbi Ḥiyya, and he ruled that the ḥalitza was valid.
why: The Gemara is defining the 'mistaken ḥalitza' that the Sages call valid. Following Rabbi Yoḥanan it means a ḥalitza done on a condition of payment, and this incident is cited from a baraita in support.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: The Sage before whom the case came; he validated the ḥalitza.

terms.meaning: The ceremony in which a childless widow removes the shoe of her late husband's brother, freeing her to marry someone else.
The brother of a man who died childless, who is obligated either to marry the widow or to release her through ḥalitza.
A silver coin; two hundred dinars was a substantial sum.

note: A man came before Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba wanting to marry his brother's widow. When the Sage told her to stand, she said her sitting was her standing; asked whether she knew the man, she said he had seen money in her and wanted to consume it, and she confirmed she did not want him. Rabbi Ḥiyya told the man, 'Let her remove your shoe, and by this you will marry her.' After she did, he told him: now she is forbidden to you anyway, so perform a proper ḥalitza so she may marry others.
why: Reish Lakish defined a valid mistaken ḥalitza as telling the brother that ḥalitza would marry him, and Rabbi Yoḥanan rejected it. Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba uses exactly that ploy and then adds a proper second ḥalitza.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba
people.about: The Sage who hears the case and steers the brother into releasing the widow.

terms.meaning: The ceremony in which a childless widow removes the shoe of her late husband's brother, freeing her to marry someone else and forbidding her to him.
A childless widow bound to her late husband's brother under the law of levirate marriage.

note: Rav Pappa's sister-in-law was bound to her late husband's brother, who was not suitable for her. Abaye told the man, 'Let her remove your shoe, and by this you will marry her.' Rav Pappa objected that this goes against Rabbi Yoḥanan, and when Abaye asked what else to say, he proposed ḥalitza on condition that she pay two hundred dinars. Afterward Abaye told her to pay, but Rav Pappa said she could claim 'I was fooling you,' citing a teaching about an escaping prisoner who promises a ferryman a dinar yet owes only the usual fare. Abaye then asked Rav Pappa where his father and mother were. 'In the city,' he said. Abaye set his eyes on them, and they died.
why: The Gemara is discussing which mistaken ḥalitza counts. This case puts Rabbi Yoḥanan's version, ḥalitza on condition of payment, into practice and shows the woman need not actually pay.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The woman's brother-in-law, who corrects Abaye's handling of the case.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage before whom the case came.

terms.meaning: The ceremony in which a childless widow removes the shoe of her late husband's brother, freeing her to marry someone else.
The brother of a man who died childless, obligated to marry the widow or release her through ḥalitza.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

note: Rav Ashi found Rav Kahana struggling to prompt a widow to recite 'He did not wish to consummate the levirate marriage' as one unbroken phrase. Rav Ashi asked whether he did not hold Rava's view that such a pause does not matter. Rav Kahana answered that Rava concedes in the case of this phrase, and quoted Abaye's wording for the bill of ḥalitza, recording which verses she and the brother were each prompted to recite.
why: Abaye said the prompter must not split 'He did not' from 'wish to consummate', and Rava called such a split a mere pause. This exchange marks where Rava's leniency stops.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Questions Rav Kahana's insistence on an unbroken recitation.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Prompts the widow at a ḥalitza ceremony and defends his care.

terms.meaning: The biblical duty of a man to marry the widow of his brother who died childless, unless he releases her through the shoe-removal ceremony of ḥalitza.
A document the court writes recording that the ḥalitza ceremony took place, so the widow can prove she is free to remarry.

note: The daughters-in-law of Abdan rebelled against their husbands. Rabbi sent a pair of Sages to examine them. Some women said to them, 'Look, your husbands are coming,' and they answered, 'Let them be your husbands.'
why: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's rule, that a minor's betrothal to another man counts as refusing her husband, applies even if she was married. Rabbi calls this reply the greatest refusal, but the Gemara says they were only betrothed.

people.name: Abdan
people.about: The father-in-law of the young wives who reject their husbands.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who sends two Sages to examine the women.

terms.meaning: Here, the young wives refused to stay married to their husbands; a girl married off as a minor could end the marriage by refusing.

flag: The story stops at the women's reply; Rabbi's verdict on it ('There is no greater refusal than this') sits in the next segment, outside the boundary.

note: In a time of danger a ruling was needed: may a girl who left her first husband by a bill of divorce, and her second by refusal, return to the first? Those involved hired a man for four hundred dinars to carry the question. He asked Rabbi Akiva, who was in prison, and he forbade it; he asked Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in Netzivin, and he forbade it too. Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, reads this into the verse 'We have drunk our water for money.'
why: The Gemara asks which early Sage holds that a minor's refusal of a later husband does not undo an earlier divorce. Rav's report names Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Asked the question while in prison and ruled it forbidden.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: Asked the question in Netzivin and also ruled it forbidden.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Tells the incident in Rav's name.

terms.meaning: A girl married off as a minor could annul the marriage by declaring that she refuses her husband, without a bill of divorce.
The document (get) a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.
A period of persecution when teaching and asking about Jewish law was itself dangerous.

note: In this telling, the question was whether a minor could refuse her marriage after her husband's death so that levirate marriage could go ahead. Those involved hired two men for four hundred dinars. They asked Rabbi Akiva in prison, and he forbade it; they asked Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in Netzivin, and he forbade it too.
why: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, says the question in Rav's version was too obvious to need asking, and gives this version instead, about refusal after the husband's death.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Asked the question while in prison and ruled it forbidden.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: Asked the question in Netzivin and also ruled it forbidden.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; four hundred dinars was a large fee, reflecting the danger of the errand.

flag: A one-line second telling of the incident just before it; the question it answers sits only in the preceding segment.

note: In the city of Neresh a girl was betrothed as a minor. After she came of age her husband seated her in the bridal chair, and another man came and snatched her from him. Rav's students Rav Bruna and Rav Ḥananel were there and did not require a bill of divorce from the second man. Rav Pappa explains that in Neresh couples consummate the marriage before the bridal chair; Rav Ashi says the snatcher acted improperly, so the Sages annulled his betrothal. When Ravina asks what happens if he betrothed her by intercourse, the Gemara answers that the Sages made his act a licentious one.
why: The Gemara is testing Rav's view that a minor's betrothal holds once she grows up only if her husband then has intercourse with her. This incident, judged by his own students, seems to contradict it.

people.name: Rav Bruna
people.about: A student of Rav, present at the incident.

people.name: Rav Ḥananel
people.about: A student of Rav, present at the incident.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Explains the incident by the custom of Neresh.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Explains that the Sages annulled the snatcher's betrothal.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Challenges Rav Ashi's explanation.

terms.meaning: The first, legally binding stage of Jewish marriage; it can be made with money or by intercourse and needs a divorce to undo.
A seat of honor where the bride was placed as part of the wedding.
The document (get) a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.

note: Rav Yitzḥak bar Bisna lost the keys to the study hall in the public domain on Shabbat, when carrying there is forbidden. He came to Rabbi Pedat, who told him to bring boys and girls to walk around there, so that if they found the keys they would bring them. The Gemara infers that Rabbi Pedat holds a court need not stop a child from breaking a prohibition; Abaye then shows that a teaching offered in support does not prove it.
why: The incident opens a discussion of whether adults must stop a child from breaking a prohibition, which the Gemara goes on to test against other teachings.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak bar Bisna
people.about: Lost the study hall keys on Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Pedat
people.about: Advised letting children find and bring the keys.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rejects the proposed proof for Rabbi Pedat's view.

terms.meaning: Open public space; carrying objects there on Shabbat is forbidden by Torah law.
An in-between area, neither fully public nor private, where carrying on Shabbat is forbidden only by rabbinic law.
A pot with no drainage hole; picking plants from it on Shabbat is forbidden only by rabbinic law.

note: At the end of a man's wedding, a fire broke out in the bridal chamber. His wife cried out, 'Look at my husband, look at my husband!' People came and saw a burnt man fallen down and the palm of a hand lying there. Rav Ḥiyya bar Avin thought to compare this to a woman who says her house was set on fire and she alone survived, whose word is not accepted. Rava rejected the comparison: there she did not cry out like this, and here there is a burnt body and a hand.
why: The Gemara is asking when a woman who reports her husband's death in a disaster is believed; it has just said a woman who survives a house fire is not, since he too may have been saved.

people.name: Rav Ḥiyya bar Avin
people.about: Would not rely on the wife's report.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Argues the wife's cry and the remains back up her report.

note: Rabbi Akiva recounts that when he went down to Neharde'a to intercalate the year, he met Neḥemya of Beit D'li. Neḥemya said he had heard that in Eretz Yisrael only Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava lets a woman remarry on the word of one witness, and Akiva confirmed it. Neḥemya told him: say to them in my name, you know this country is riddled with troops, that I received from Rabban Gamliel the Elder that a woman may marry on the word of one witness.
why: The Gemara asks whether one witness to a husband's death is believed in wartime. Rami bar Ḥama cites this account, and the debate turns on what Neḥemya's remark about troops means.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Tells of his meeting with Neḥemya.

people.name: Neḥemya of Beit D'li
people.about: A Sage in Neharde'a who passes on a tradition from Rabban Gamliel the Elder.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
people.about: Said to be the only Sage in Eretz Yisrael relying on one witness.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel the Elder
people.about: The source of Neḥemya's tradition.

people.name: Rami bar Ḥama
people.about: Brings this account into the discussion.

terms.meaning: To add a leap month to the Jewish calendar so the festivals stay in their seasons, a decision made by the Sages.
The Land of Israel.

note: Two Torah scholars were traveling by boat with Abba Yosei ben Simai, and the boat sank. Rabbi allowed their wives to remarry on the testimony of women.
why: The Gemara asks whether one witness to a death is believed in wartime. Water is treated like war, and many women count as one witness, so this seems to say yes; the Gemara answers that the women gave identifying marks.

people.name: Abba Yosei ben Simai
people.about: Was traveling on the boat with the two scholars.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who allowed the widows to remarry.

note: Yitzḥak the Exilarch, son of Rav Beivai's sister, was traveling from Cortva to Spain and died. A message came from Spain reporting his death by name. The question was whether to worry that there were two men named Yitzḥak. Abaye said we are concerned; Rava said we are not. The text does not give the outcome.
why: The Gemara has just debated whether a labelled container may hold something other than its label says; the same doubt is now asked of a name, and Abaye and Rava go on to defend their views with other cases.

people.name: Yitzḥak the Exilarch
people.about: The man reported dead on the road to Spain.

people.name: Rav Beivai
people.about: Yitzḥak's uncle; Yitzḥak is his sister's son.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Holds we must worry about another man of the same name.
