people.name: Rava
people.about: Holds we need not worry about that.

terms.meaning: The title of the head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

note: Shmuel tells that at the end of the wheat harvest ten men went out to reap. A snake bit one of them and he died. His wife came and told the court, and they sent messengers who found it was as she said. At that time they ruled that a woman who says 'My husband died' may remarry, or enter levirate marriage.
why: Beit Hillel hold that a woman's word about her husband's death is accepted only in circumstances like the original incident, Beit Shammai that it extends further; the Gemara asks what that incident was.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage whose account of the incident Rav Yehuda reports.

terms.meaning: The biblical duty of a man to marry the widow of his brother who died childless.

note: A man was carrying waters and ashes of purification across the Jordan River in a boat, and an olive-bulk of a corpse was found stuck to the bottom of the boat. At that time the Sages ruled that no one may carry waters and ashes of purification across the Jordan in a boat.
why: Rabbi Ḥananya ben Akiva limits that decree to the Jordan and to boats, as in the incident, while the Rabbis apply it to all rivers; the Gemara compares this to the dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.

terms.meaning: The ashes of the red heifer and water mixed with them, used to purify people who had become impure through contact with the dead; they had to be kept pure themselves.
A piece of a dead body the size of an olive, the smallest amount that transmits the impurity of the dead.

note: Abba bar Marta, also called Abba bar Minyumi, owed money to members of the Exilarch's household. He took wax, stuck it to a strip of worn-out cloth and stuck that to his forehead. He passed in front of them, and they did not recognize him.
why: A teaching just quoted says witnesses may identify a dead man only if they saw both his forehead and his face with the nose; this incident shows that changing the forehead alone can make a man unrecognizable.

people.name: Abba bar Marta
people.about: Also called Abba bar Minyumi; disguises himself from those he owes money.

terms.meaning: The title of the head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

note: In Asya, people lowered a man into the sea on a rope, and when they pulled it back only his leg came up in their hands. The Sages ruled that if the leg was cut off from the knee up, his wife may remarry; if from the knee down, she may not.
why: The Gemara proposed that the Mishna's rule against testifying about a man cut open follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who says such a wound can heal. This incident treats a high cut as fatal and seems to contradict that; the Gemara answers that water aggravates a wound.

note: A man drowned at Carmi and was pulled out near Bei Hedya after three days, and Rav Dimi of Neharde'a allowed his wife to remarry. Another man drowned in the Tigris and was pulled out at the Bridge of Shabistana, and Rava allowed his wife to remarry on the testimony of his friends, five days after his death.
why: The Mishna allows identifying a body only within three days, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava disputes it; the Gemara asks whether he is more lenient or more strict. These rulings fit the lenient reading, but the Gemara answers that water keeps the body from changing.

people.name: Rav Dimi from Neharde'a
people.about: Allowed the first drowned man's wife to remarry.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Allowed the second drowned man's wife to remarry.

note: A man drowned in the lake of Samkei, and Rav Sheila allowed his wife to remarry. Rav said to Shmuel, 'Come, let us excommunicate him.' Shmuel said, 'Let us first send to him.' They asked him whether a wife is forbidden when her husband disappears in water with no visible end; he said she is forbidden, and that the lake of Samkei is such water. Asked why he had acted as he did, he answered: 'I erred. I thought still water counts as water with an end, but because there are waves, the waves may have carried him off.' Shmuel applied to Rav the verse 'No mischief shall befall the righteous,' and Rav applied to Shmuel 'Salvation lies in much counsel.'
why: The Rabbis permit the wife only if the water has a visible end, and Abaye has just defined that as water whose shore can be seen on all four sides; this case shows a judge misapplying the rule.

people.name: Rav Sheila
people.about: Allowed the drowned man's wife to remarry, then admitted he had erred.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Wanted to excommunicate Rav Sheila for the ruling.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Advised Rav to ask Rav Sheila first.

terms.meaning: To place a person under a formal ban that cuts him off from the community, a sanction the Sages used against those who defied their rulings.
A body of water so large that its shore cannot be seen on every side, so a man who went under might have come out unseen elsewhere.

note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi tells of two men fishing with nets on the Jordan River. One went into a cave by the shore where fish gathered, the sun set, and in the dark he could not find the way out. His friend waited long enough to be sure he had died, then went and told the man's household. The next morning the sun rose, the man saw the opening, came out, and arrived home to find a great eulogy under way for him. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said: how great are the words of the Sages, who ruled that if a man is lost in water with a visible end his wife may remarry, but if the water has no visible end she may not.
why: The discussion has just dealt with Rav Sheila, who let a wife remarry after her husband vanished in the lake of Samkei, then admitted his error because waves could carry a man out of sight. This incident shows why the Sages refuse to presume death when a man disappears in such water.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Tells the incident and draws the lesson from it.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first great collection of Jewish law. The Gemara often quotes one to support or challenge a point.

A body of water whose shores can all be seen from where the man went under. If he does not come up, witnesses would have seen him climb out somewhere, so his death can be presumed. In water with no visible end he might have come out unseen.

note: Rabban Gamliel recalls traveling on a boat and seeing another boat break apart and sink. He grieved for the Torah scholar aboard, Rabbi Akiva. But when Rabban Gamliel reached dry land, Rabbi Akiva came, sat down and debated Jewish law before him. Asked who had brought him up, Rabbi Akiva said a plank from the ship came to him, and he bowed his head to every wave that came at him. From this, the Sages said that when wicked people come upon a person he should bow his head before them. Rabban Gamliel said that at that moment he thought: how great are the words of the Sages, who said a wife may remarry when her husband is lost in water with a visible end, but not when the water has no end.
why: The Gemara has just rejected Rav Ashi's idea that a Torah scholar's survival would surely become known, ruling that no one lost in endless water is presumed dead. This is one of several accounts of men seen lost at sea who came back alive.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Tells the story; he watched the ship sink and later met the survivor.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Torah scholar on the sinking ship, who survived by clinging to a plank.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first great collection of Jewish law.
Jewish law. To deliberate about halakha is to debate legal questions, as students did before their teachers.
A body of water whose shores cannot all be seen. A man who goes under there might come out somewhere unseen, so the Sages do not let his wife remarry on the assumption that he drowned.

note: Rabbi Akiva recalls traveling on a boat and seeing another boat tossed and sinking at sea. He grieved for the Torah scholar aboard, Rabbi Meir. But when Rabbi Akiva landed in the province of Cappadocia, Rabbi Meir came, sat down and debated Jewish law before him. Asked who had brought him up, Rabbi Meir said one wave tossed him to the next, and that one to the next, until a wave threw him up onto dry land. Rabbi Akiva said that at that moment he thought: how great are the words of the Sages, who said a wife may remarry when her husband is lost in water with a visible end, but not when the water has no end.
why: This follows Rabban Gamliel's account of Rabbi Akiva surviving a shipwreck, as a second case of a man seen lost at sea who came back alive, backing the rule that a wife may not remarry when her husband vanished in endless water.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Tells the story; he saw the ship sink and later met the survivor in Cappadocia.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Torah scholar on the sinking ship, carried ashore by the waves.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first great collection of Jewish law.
A body of water whose shores cannot all be seen. A man who goes under there might come out somewhere unseen, so the Sages do not let his wife remarry on the assumption that he drowned.

note: The daughter of Neḥunya the well digger fell into the Great Cistern, and people came to tell Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa. After the first hour he told them: peace. After the second: peace. After the third: she has come up. He asked the girl who had pulled her up, and she said a ram came by, with an old man leading it. They asked Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa whether he was a prophet. He answered with the verse 'I am not a prophet, nor the son of a prophet,' and explained his reasoning: could the children of a righteous man come to harm through the very work he labors at?
why: The mishna cited Rabbi Meir's case of a man who came out of the Great Cistern alive after three days, and the Sages objected that miracles are not used to set law. The Gemara then tells of another rescue from the same cistern; right after, Rabbi Abba notes that Neḥunya's son still died of thirst.

people.name: Neḥunya the well digger
people.about: Father of the girl; Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa calls him righteous for his work digging water sources.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa
people.about: The Sage the people turn to; he tells them hour by hour that the girl is safe, and then that she is out.

terms.meaning: A large cistern for storing water, also named in the mishna's earlier case of a man who fell into it.

note: A gentile went around calling out: Who is from the house of Ḥivvai? Who is from the house of Ḥivvai? Ḥivvai has died. On the strength of this, Rav Yosef allowed Ḥivvai's wife to marry. Another gentile went around saying: Alas for the brave horseman who was in Pumbedita, for he is dead. Rav Yosef, and some say Rava, allowed his wife to marry.
why: The mishna says a gentile who intends to testify is not believed. After learning that the Rabbis rejected Rabbi Oshaya's wider use of gentile testimony, the Gemara asks when a gentile is ever believed, and answers: when he speaks offhandedly, as in these two cases.

people.name: Ḥivvai
people.about: A man reported dead by a gentile calling out in the street.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who allowed the wives to remarry on the gentiles' reports.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Named in one version as the Sage who ruled in the horseman's case.

terms.meaning: Mentioning something in passing, with no aim of giving testimony or affecting a court's decision. A gentile's report of a death is believed only when said this way.
The first great written collection of Jewish law; the Gemara is the long discussion built around it.

note: A gentile went around calling: Who is from the house of Ḥasa? Ḥasa has drowned. Rav Naḥman exclaimed: By God! The fish have eaten Ḥasa. Because of what Rav Naḥman said, Ḥasa's wife went and married, and no one said anything to her. Rav Ashi learned from this that a remarriage after a husband vanished in water with no visible end is not undone once it has happened. Others tell it differently: Rav Naḥman actually allowed her to marry, reasoning that Ḥasa was a great man, so if he had come out alive the news would have spread. The Gemara rejects that reasoning: great man or not, the marriage stands after the fact but is not allowed beforehand.
why: It continues the cases of a gentile's offhand report of a death. Here the man drowned, so the case also tests the rule that a wife may not remarry when her husband vanished in endless water.

people.name: Ḥasa
people.about: A man reported drowned by a gentile; called a great man in one version.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage whose exclamation, or in another version his ruling, led to Ḥasa's wife remarrying.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Draws the legal lesson from the case.

terms.meaning: From the outset, before the act. Something not allowed ab initio may still be allowed to stand after the fact, once it has been done.
A body of water whose shores cannot all be seen. A man who goes under there might come out unseen, so his death is not presumed.

note: A gentile told a Jew: Cut fodder and give it to my animals on Shabbat, or I will kill you as I killed so-and-so the Jew, who would not cook me a pot of food on Shabbat. The dead man's wife heard this and came before Abaye. He put off her case through three pilgrim festivals. Rav Adda bar Ahava told her: Go to Rav Yosef, whose knife is sharp. She went, and Rav Yosef settled it from a teaching: a gentile selling fruit at market who says his fruit is forbidden produce has said nothing, since he only meant to make his goods look better. The translation explains that Rav Yosef therefore would not rely on the gentile's claim.
why: The Gemara has shown that a gentile who mentions a death offhandedly is believed. This case asks about a gentile who speaks for his own purposes, here to frighten someone.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The first Sage the widow asks; he delays his ruling through three festivals.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: Sends the woman on to Rav Yosef.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage 'whose knife is sharp', who resolves her case.

terms.meaning: Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot. The translation notes that Sages gathered to study on these festivals, so a hard question could be raised before many of them.
Fruit from a tree's first three years of growth, which Jewish law forbids eating.
A figure of speech for a sharp legal mind who can cut through a hard question.

note: Abba Yudan of Sidon reports that a Jew and a gentile traveled the road together. Later the gentile came back and said: Alas for the Jew who was with me on the road, for he died on the way, and I buried him. On this statement, the Jew's wife was allowed to marry.
why: Rav Yosef has just refused to rely on a gentile who spoke with his own aims. This report gives the other side: a gentile who mentions a death in passing, in a lament, is believed, and the widow may remarry.

people.name: Abba Yudan of Sidon
people.about: Reports the incident.

note: A group of men chained together by collars was being marched to Antokhya. A gentile later came and said: Alas for the collared people, for they died, and I buried them. Their wives were allowed to marry. In another incident, sixty men were walking to the siege of Beitar. A gentile came and said: Alas for those sixty people walking on the road to Beitar, for they died, and I buried them. Their wives too were allowed to marry.
why: These continue Abba Yudan of Sidon's list of cases in which a gentile's passing lament over the dead was trusted enough to let the widows remarry.

terms.meaning: A collar. The translation explains these were prisoners, each chained by a collar around the neck.
A siege. Here, the siege of the city of Beitar.

note: A man came before Rabbi Tarfon to testify that a woman's husband had died. Asked how he knew, he said they were traveling together when a troop of soldiers chased them; the husband grabbed an olive branch, tore it off and drove the troop back. 'Lion, well done,' the witness said to him, and the husband asked how he knew his name was Lion: in his town he was called Yoḥanan son of Rabbi Yehonatan, the lion of Kefar Shiḥayya. Later he fell ill and died, and Rabbi Tarfon let the wife marry. In a second version the branch is a fig branch, and Rabbi Tarfon tests the witness by misstating the name. The witness corrects him, keeps his story straight two or three times, and only then does Rabbi Tarfon let the wife marry.
why: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Tarfon demands formal cross-examination of witnesses to a husband's death, since the second version has him question the witness and the first does not. It answers that the point is disputed: Rabbi Akiva says it is not needed, Rabbi Tarfon says it is.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: The judge who hears the witness and allows the widow to marry.

people.name: Yoḥanan, son of Rabbi Yehonatan
people.about: The dead husband, known in his town as the lion; in the second version called Yoḥanan son of Yonatan.

terms.meaning: The formal cross-examination of witnesses that a court uses to test testimony, checking details for consistency.
Hebrew for lion. The witness used it as praise, and it turned out to be the man's nickname.
